                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft is offering another year of Windows 10 security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027.
                                            If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action.
                                            Other users can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you are still holding on to Windows 10, there's good news: Microsoft is offering another year of security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027. Microsoft officially ended support for the older OS last year but allowed users to join the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in order to maintain protection against viruses and hackers. ESU coverage was supposed to expire on Oct. 13, 2026, but the company is allowing enrolled Windows 10 users to receive monthly patches for another year—and it's not too late to sign up if you haven't already.  You can stay on Windows 10 through Oct. 2027If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action on your part. If you haven't, though, you can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year. To be eligible, your device must be running Windows 10 version 22H2 Home, Professional, Pro Education, or Workstations editions and have the latest Windows update installed. You must also be signed into a Microsoft account with administrator status. 
Windows users were originally able to purchase ESU coverage for $30, and Microsoft later added the option to either redeem 1,000 Microsoft Rewards points or opt into Windows Backup to get protection for free. To check your coverage or sign up, go to Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update and look for an ESU enrollment link (visible if your device is eligible). Follow the prompts to sign into your Microsoft account and choose your enrollment option. If you've already purchased an ESU license, you can apply it to up to 10 devices running Windows 10 as long as they are linked to your Microsoft account. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The ESU program does not include any new features or non-security updates, but if you want to stay on Windows 10, it's highly recommended that you enroll in the program. Microsoft has started pushing hundreds of critical security fixes each month—a handful of which have been actively exploited zero-days—so you should ensure your device stays protected for as long as possible.

title: I Tried Snap Specs, and They Could Be the Future of Smart Glasses
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”

            Credit: Stephen Johnson
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Snap was in the smart glasses game from the jump. The company’s original camera-equipped Spectacles debuted back in 2016, beating Meta to the market by five years. Meta’s Ray-Bans and Oakleys captured massive consumer mindshare anyway, while Snap’s smart eyewear has been less visible. With Snap Specs, though, the company is aiming to make up for lost time by delivering smart glasses that go beyond a hidden camera and voice-activated AI. At the Snapdragon 2026 Summit, I got my hands (and eyes) on a pair of Snap’s soon-to-be-released spatial-computing glasses that overlay digital graphics onto the physical world.Specs are heavy on tech but light on your face
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
There's a lot of tech packed into these black polymer frames. They're powered by two Snapdragon processors, with two full-color hi-res cameras facing outward; the tracking system supports 6DOF (six degrees of freedom) hand tracking for gesture controls; and it's all standalone, as there's no tether or wired puck handling the heavy lifting. With all that crammed into the frames, plus the battery to run it, you'd expect them to be heavy. At around 135 grams, they aren’t light, but Specs are surprisingly comfortable. The weight is distributed evenly, mainly across the frames, so for the brief time I used them, they remained ergonomically acceptable. Specs feel more like a pair of sunglasses than a bulky VR helmet. As for battery life, Snap promises four hours of mixed-use on a full charge. 
Display quality on Snap SpecsIn the interest of not alienating the people around you, Snap chose to make the lenses clear enough that your eyes can still be seen through them, but if you want to close out the world, there’s electrochromic dimming for quick transitions between clear and dark lenses. It both useful and a cool trick. Check it out:
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
The in-glasses display is surprisingly bright. Specs' visuals are powered by a proprietary liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) display system, and even when used in a light-filled conference room, I could still clearly see the UI and its various apps. I tested out YouTube under these borderline abusive conditions, and it streamed high-def video in 16 million colors suitably.  The display offers a 51-degree field of view. It feels like having a large floating window hovering in front of you. From there, you can use simple gestures to launch apps, watch movies, play games, and do most other tasks you can’t do from your phone. But it was the context-aware, real-world spatial computing tasks that I wanted to try—the things you can't do from a phone or PC. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What can you actually do with a pair of Snap Specs? Snap plans to launch Specs with a full suite of both first-party and third-party apps that will do everything from improving your drawing skills to teaching you music. I tried out a golfing demo, and it made the possibilities of augmented reality glasses immediately clear. Instead of putting blindly toward a distant hole, Specs show you exactly which direction to swing the putter and adds a virtual flag to mark where the hole is. It’s anecdotal evidence, but my personal putting game improved immensely. Is it cheating? Probably, but it works. Are Specs going to be useful in the real world?A half-hour or so of testing a prototype isn’t enough time to really say whether these will be useful in a person’s real life, but I can say for sure that they’re very cool, and I’m looking forward to going more in-depth with them in the coming months as their release date approaches. Snap Specs are planned for release this fall and will retail for $2,195. (Thanks to Qualcomm for the trip to check out these glasses at Snapdragon Summit 2026)

                Key Takeaways
                                            Spotify and Claude are both down Tuesday morning.
                                            Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports for each platform.
                                            Spotfiy confirmed the outage in a post on X, while Anthropic confirm issues on its Claude status page.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're having trouble getting your Spotify playlists up and running this morning, you're not alone. The music streaming platform is currently down for tens of thousands of users, at least. Downdetector is showing roughly 40,000 reports since 9:31 a.m. ET, with the last batch of reports coming in at 10:24 a.m. Spotify confirmed the issue in a post on X, writing: "We're aware of some issues right now and are checking them out!" Curiously, Spotify's outage comes at the same time as an outage with Claude, the AI platform from Anthropic. Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports here as well, and Anthropic confirmed an ongoing issue with Claude: "We are investigating reports of degraded performance affecting claude.ai, platform.claude.com, the Claude API, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. We will provide an update as soon as possible."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear why these services are down this morning, or if they are related. But in all likelihood, Spotify and Anthropic will get their platforms back up and running soon. Typically, these occasional outages are resolved in hours, if not minutes, barring a widespread problem, like an outage with a cloud hosting provider. Last year's AWS outage "broke the internet," as did November's Cloudflare outage. There's no reason to think that's the case with these outages at this time.

        Homebrew is the package manager you wish your Mac shipped with. Once you set it up, Homebrew lets you install and update apps quickly and securely. It launched as a command-line interface, where you would type commands into the Terminal app on your Mac to install, update, or uninstall your apps. Recently, Homebrew launched its own GUI, which makes it easier than ever to use the service. Here are 10 Homebrew hacks that you should know, great for new and legacy users alike.
Try Homebrew's new GUI to discover apps
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
Once you update to Homebrew version 7.0.0 or newer, you'll notice that the service has a new GUI-enabled app for your Mac. You can launch it like any other app from the Applications folder, and use the interface to discover, install, update, and remove apps. The left pane has a few tabs that allow you to keep tabs on apps you've installed via Homebrew, updates available for those apps, fixes for issues with installation, and Homebrew settings. It also has an option called "Discover," which lets you search for apps available to install via Homebrew. Just use the search bar to look for your favorite apps, and if they show up, click the "Install" button. This will download that app to your Mac, and automatically complete the installation.Check out Homebrew's "doctor" to fix software issuesHomebrew has a "doctor" feature that lets you fix issues with the service. This can be anything from unsupported or deprecated apps, to issues with the Homebrew configuration itself. You can run this from the "Doctor" tab in the Homebrew GUI, or use the following command via Terminal:
brew drThe service will recommend some fixes, and you can run the suggested command in Terminal to solve the problem.Use the -q suffix to keep Terminal free of clutterWhen you're using Homebrew via Terminal, you'll quickly notice that every action leaves you with a wall of text. This is great for those who want to track all those updates, or those who are roleplaying as characters from The Matrix, but not for everyone. If you want Homebrew to do its work quietly, just add the "-q" suffix to your commands. For example:brew install firefox -qThis will minimize the number of text updates on-screen, and leave you with a much cleaner Terminal. If you'd like to see more updates, you can replace "-q" with "-v" at the end of the command.Try the "list" command to view all installed apps via Terminal
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
If you're not using Homebrew's GUI, it's easy to forget which apps you installed via Homebrew, and which ones are outside of it. To solve this, use the following command to show a list of all apps installed via Homebrew:brew listUse this command to add manually installed apps to HomebrewIf you're like me, you've probably installed some apps via Homebrew, and downloaded a few others from the developers' websites. This means you can't update all your apps in one go, since some of them are not managed by Homebrew. You can fix this issue by adopting those apps into Homebrew. Use the following command to get this done:brew install cask adopt APPNAMEAs long as the apps are supported in Homebrew, this command will adopt them into the service. You can confirm the adoption by using the "brew list" command mentioned above.Use the cleanup command to free up storage spaceWhen you install a lot of apps via Homebrew, it tends to create some clutter. Old versions of apps and cached downloads aren't always deleted immediately. If you're running short on space, you can try the following cleanup command to free up space without deleting apps:brew cleanupUse this Homebrew command to update all apps in one goThis is one of the best features in Homebrew, and it works best right after a new version of macOS is released. This is when a flurry of app updates arrives to support the new operating system, and you can try this command to update all Homebrew apps in one go:brew upgradeIn case you just want to see which apps need an update, you can try this command:brew outdatedThe upgrade command is also listed under the "Upgrades" tab in the Homebrew GUI.Use "dry run" to check which packages will be installed or updatedIf you add the "dry run" flag to any install or update command, it will reveal a list of planned updates without commencing the installation. When you're dealing with command-line interfaces, "dry run" can be a useful way to preview changes before they take place, and to ensure that the correct app is being installed or updated. This is how you can use it:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
brew install APPNAME --dry-runSet up aliases to avoid typing long commandsIf you're tired of typing long commands in Homebrew, you can set up aliases to minimize keystrokes. For instance, you can use "brew i" instead of "brew install" to update all Homebrew apps. Use this command to set this up:brew alias i='install'Feel free to set up aliases for as many Homebrew commands as you like. The following command will list all the aliases you've set up:brew aliasTo remove an alias, use this command:brew unalias iJust remember to replace "i" with whichever alias you wish to remove.Use this command to stop specific apps from updatingIf you don't want to update to the newest versions of certain apps, you can use the "pin" command to stop updates, and then "unpin" when you are ready to update again. This can be useful when an app you trust gets acquired by new owners who have yet to prove themselves, or if it adds new features you don't want, etc. Here's how to use it:brew pin APPNAMEWhen you're ready to update it again, try this:brew unpin APPNAMENote that you may also have to disable auto-updates from the app's interface separately because some apps just update themselves without confirmation.

title: Why Your 'HIIT' Workouts Are Full of Empty Promises
description: High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, made headlines in the 2010s with one specific claim: that short bursts of hard work can g
body:
High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, made headlines in the 2010s with one specific claim: that short bursts of hard work can give the same aerobic benefits as longer sessions of jogging or cycling. But the HIIT videos you can stream today have very little to do with the original model, and many of them aren’t worth your time. Before we break down the difference, I want to make something clear: If you love doing videos labeled “HIIT,” and they’re part of an exercise routine that makes you genuinely happy, keep on doing them. I’m not trying to take away a thing that you love. But if you’re doing them because you feel  they’re the best way to achieve your goals, or because a trainer or influencer tells you that they’ll burn a ton of calories or build your booty, we need to sit down for a little intervention. 
What is "real" HIIT?High-intensity interval training was born as a buzzword after exercise scientists noticed that people got better at the Wingate test every time they took it. The Wingate protocol calls for people to pedal a stationary bike all-out, at a high resistance, for a pukeworthy 30 seconds. Then you get to rest for four minutes, and do it again. After further experiments, researchers figured out that the benefits they saw, including increased aerobic fitness, could be triggered by other rest/work combinations. The Tabata protocol, again done on a research-grade exercise bike (“cycle ergometer,” they call it) is 20 seconds of work and 10 seconds of rest, repeated "seven to eight times" to achieve exhaustion in the original study—or about four minutes in total. These are not workouts that people do for fun. Everyone I’ve seen recount the experience has said that it was complete agony. The scientists often note that people can rarely push themselves hard enough to replicate these protocols on their own. Workout classes and videos don't push you that hard, either. Peloton offers "Tabata" classes that ask you to do those four-minute blocks several times in the same workout, meaning you definitely didn't push yourself to exhaustion on the first one. To create a more accessible version of HIIT, Martin Gibala, one of the researchers who popularized the concept of HIIT, worked to find a version of the protocol that normal humans could do on their own, and that wouldn’t leave them so pooped they were scared to come back. His conclusion: one minute work/one minute rest was the sweet spot, and you could do it while cycling, jogging, or doing other aerobic activities. Interval workouts boomed in popularity, using a variety of work/rest intervals.Another accessible version of HIIT is the Norwegian 4x4, which uses four-minute intervals at a hard but not exhaustive effort, with three minutes' rest in between, repeated four times. This takes longer than the HIIT protocols I mention above—about 40 minutes for a complete workout—but it's been shown to be effective for cardio gains.How do newer HIIT videos compare?The term HIIT didn’t just get watered down; it mutated. When it began, HIIT was about getting more results in less time, so it built a reputation as being more efficient, maybe even superior to things like jogging. And since you don’t need a bike to do HIIT, trainers ran with that idea and started applying the term to literally anything they could think of. Bodyweight squats? Bicep curls? Sure, why not. As a result, these days HIIT means something more like “a workout video with a timer counting down in the corner.”HIIT’s popularity had been building for years when COVID hit, and from there it exploded. If you’re a trainer or influencer trying to come up with something you can easily film, you’ll probably gravitate to no-equipment home workouts. And to make them sound exciting, you’ll call them HIIT.I suspect the label “HIIT” on a bodyweight workout is supposed to translate as “good enough.” Yeah, you’re doing a few lunges in your living room, but the trainer wants you to think it’s just as good as anything you could get from a boutique studio or a full-featured gym. Maybe better. For any reason you might want to work out—burning calories 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
"HIIT" workout promises you can't trustYou can tell how far removed these workouts are from real HIIT by judging the promises they make. Are they saying they’ll improve your VO2max, which was one of the original benefits noted? They won’t—not usually. Let’s do a quick rundown: Do they burn a lot of calories? Not necessarily, but it depends on the workout. The longer the workout and the more out of breath you are, the more calories you’re burning. The truth is, 20 minutes of “HIIT” often doesn’t burn any more than 20 minutes of medium-intensity exercise like jogging. Do they burn more calories after the workout? In theory, your body keeps burning calories after a hard workout session. But there are two caveats: First, this is only significant when the workout is really intense. Second, after you do a hard workout, your body often wants to conserve calories for the rest of the day, so it all evens out while you’re lying on the couch. Even Gibala has said that afterburn is overstated.Do they help you lose weight? Diet matters more to weight loss than the amount of exercise you do, much less the specific type. Exercise can help a little bit with the “calories burned” side of the equation (as long as it doesn’t make you hungrier, which it sometimes does), but now we’re back to the reality that HIIT workouts don’t offer any special advantage in burning calories.Do they build muscle? Maybe a little, but they won’t get you the booty/arms/whatever of your dreams. You optimize muscle growth with strength training routines that ask you to lift heavy and then rest until you're recovered again—usually at least one minute, often longer. "HIIT" workouts that keep you moving the whole time, or that only have short rests, can build some muscle, but pretty soon you’ll be strong enough that the workout isn’t challenging your muscles enough to grow. You really do need to train increasingly heavy if you want to build muscle.How do I know if an HIIT video is actually good?First, ask yourself why you’re doing the video. Do you want to increase your aerobic fitness? Then evaluate whether following the video actually gets you out of breath and allows adequate rest for you to do it again. Do you want to build muscle? Then evaluate whether the video actually challenges your muscles.As I mentioned above, sometimes we do “HIIT” videos not for any specific outcome, but because it feels good to move our bodies and we like the moves in the video. This is fine and good, and it definitely counts toward the 75 to 150 minutes of exercise you should be getting weekly. But if you have specific goals, seek out the best ways to achieve them. Chances are, there’s something out there that’s better for you than yet another “HIIT” video.

title: Your Fitness Tracker Has No Idea How Many Calories You’re Burning
body:
It would be great if Fitbits and Apple Watches were accurate, but sorry—they're not.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 22, 2026
                
            
    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            
                        Credit: Composite / Alisa Stern; Shutterstock / Prostock-studio
                            
    
            
            
        
            Here are all the ways to find the right fitness wearable for you, and how to make the most of the data it can offer.
        
    
    
        
        When I test smartwatches and fitness trackers, I place a particular emphasis on accuracy. Is my running pace correct? Does the device capture the ups and downs of my heart rate? I even got a VO2max lab test to check a bunch of watches' fitness scores. But one thing I never test for accuracy is calorie burn. None of my devices come close to agreeing on the number of calories they think I'm burning, and I don't expect them to. Even scientists who study the accuracy of wearables can't answer the question in a way that's useful when you're shopping for this year's devices—but we'll get into why that is below. There was a time, before Fitbits, when nobody knew quite how many calories they were burning on a daily basis. Sure, you could calculate a rough estimate based on your body size, sex, and age. You could choose whether or not to believe the calorie readout on the cardio machines at the gym. (You shouldn't.) But the idea that a gadget on your wrist could tell you how many calories you personally burned during one particular day was revolutionary. It was also wrong.   How fitness trackers calculate calorie burnBefore I discuss how accurate fitness trackers are, let’s look at where they get their numbers. For calorie calculations, the main sources are motion and heart rate data. For motion, trackers use accelerometers to figure out when your body is moving, and by how much. If you have a watch on your wrist, and the watch swings back and forth rhythmically while sort of bouncing up and down, your gadget guesses that you must be walking. If there is quicker bouncing and your wrist makes a smaller movement, you’re probably running. 
This is the basic idea behind how trackers detect how many steps you’re taking. If you’ve paid attention to your step count, you already know some of the ways this can be inaccurate. If you’re shopping, for example, keeping your hand on the shopping cart handle may result in you not getting credit for the steps you’re taking, though this depends on the device. (For a perfect illustration of this issue, see these tests I did comparing a Garmin to an Apple Watch on a treadmill. When I rested my hands on the treadmill handle, the Apple Watch recorded 318 steps while the Garmin recorded none.)Then there’s the heart rate sensor: Since your hands don’t always move predictably during exercise, it can be easier to just tell your watch that you’ll be cycling or doing yoga or whatever. The gadget then uses your heart rate to make an educated guess about how much work your body is doing. Whatever the source of the data—heart rate, movements, or a combination—the gadget processes it through a formula to calculate how many calories it thinks you’re burning. Your age, weight, and sex may figure into this equation. Importantly, though, the fitness tracker doesn’t actually know how many calories you’re burning; instead, it’s calculating a probable number based on incomplete information. Why there's no simple test for calorie burn accuracyIf humans were robots, all built the same, all moving in predictable patterns, this formulaic approach might work. But humans are complicated, and technology often gets confused. For example, you may get different step counts if you put a device on your right versus left wrist. And the optical heart rate sensors that a lot of trackers use may be less accurate on dark skin compared to lighter skin. These problems relate to the data that the trackers gather, but calorie burn isn't a direct measurement. It's an estimate derived from doing math with the data the watch measures, and different algorithms can come up with different calorie burn numbers depending on how the algorithm is designed. The companies that make fitness trackers aren’t required to publish their algorithms or verify that their calorie counts are accurate. They can just put a device on the market, and there you are, comparing wearables on shopping sites without any information about how accurate they are, outside of the companies’ claims.Researchers are interested in fitness trackers’ accuracy, which would seem like a good thing. They want to be able to use wearables in research or recommend them for individuals and healthcare providers, and so they'll run studies comparing consumer devices to lab equipment. This sounds like a great way to answer our questions! But there’s a huge delay in actually getting that information, and it’s often published too late to be useful. By the time a researcher buys a batch of the latest model, runs a study, writes it up, submits it to a journal, and finally gets it published, several years may have gone by, and the company has moved on to the next model. That delay is why I (usually) can't use scientific studies to weigh in on the devices I write about. Here's a great example of how frustrating it can be: This review was published in 2025, and found the Series 1 was the Apple Watch that turned up the most often in the studies the authors were able to gather. The Series 9 and 10 watches were completely missing from the available data—and as a reminder, we're now up to the Series 12. With that caveat about delays, I still think it’s useful to look at the research on fitness trackers to see what themes emerge. Are any of them good at estimating your calorie burn? What studies say about fitness trackers’ accuracyTime for the bad news. A study from 2020 that looked at a variety of gadgets from Apple, Garmin, Polar, and Fitbit found that all the devices are inaccurate more often than they are accurate. The authors considered a device to be accurate if its reading was plus or minus 3% when compared to a more reliable measure of energy expenditure (that is, calorie burn) in a lab setting. Here’s how some of the top brands fared: Garmin devices underestimated calorie burn 69% of the time.Apple watches overestimated calorie burn 58% of the time.Polar devices overestimated calorie burn 69% of the time.Fitbits underestimated calorie burn 48% of the time and overestimated 39% of the time.The fact that Fitbits were roughly correct on average doesn’t mean they were useful. If sometimes your device overestimates and sometimes it underestimates, it’s not very helpful unless you know which is which. A 2018 review specifically of Fitbits found that accuracy varied greatly depending on factors like where they were worn (torso was more accurate than wrist), whether you were walking uphill, and whether you walked at a constant speed or stopped and started. The accuracy also varied by device, with the Fitbit Classic underestimating calorie burn and the Fitbit Charge usually overestimating. The devices just aren’t accurate enough to know how many calories you’re really burning
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
A 2022 study compared the Apple Watch 6, the Fitbit Sense, and the Polar Vantage V. The researchers had volunteers wear all three gadgets while sitting quietly, walking, running, cycling, and strength training. Every gadget, for every activity, was awarded a judgment of “poor accuracy,” with coefficients of variation ranging from 15% to 30%.This 2025 review of Apple Watch studies—the same one I mention above—found that calorie burn was, on average, off by about 18%. The authors mention a proposed standard from the International Electrotechnical Commission that recommends fitness trackers not be off by more than 10%. That's clearly not being met, although the researchers noted that newer models may be more accurate than earlier ones. And this 2026 study looked specifically at how accuracy relates to skin tone and to the amount of fat a person has. To the devices' credit, skin tone didn't seem to affect calorie counts very much, but adiposity (fat content) did. The higher a volunteer's body fat percentage was, the more inaccurate their calorie burn result. The Garmin Forerunner 955 and Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 seriously overestimated calories; the Apple Watch Series 8 also overestimated but not as much; and the Fitbit Sense 2 underestimated when it wasn't producing wild outliers. The authors concluded that all devices "substantially misestimate" calorie burn during exercise.To get a sense of these percentages, let's say your true calorie burn is 2,000 calories per day. A device that's off by 15%—on the low end of what these studies found—might report that you burned 1,700 calories, or that you burned 2,300. If you're using your device to figure out how much to eat, you could be way off in meeting your calorie goals. If these devices are all inaccurate, how can you know how many calories you're burning?It’s probably most useful if you think of your calorie burn as a number you cannot measure directly. Treat it as a black box: I burn some unknowable number of calories; now what? The only common reason you would need an accurate estimate of calorie burn is if you are trying to figure out how much food you need to eat. If you want to lose weight, you want to eat less than you burn; if you want to gain weight, you want the reverse; and if you’re trying to maintain your weight, you want to eat roughly the same as what you burn. But think about it this way: you don't actually need to know your calorie burn if you have the other two terms in the equation—your calorie intake and your weight. It's considered more accurate to adjust how much to eat based directly on your weight, rather than using calorie burn estimates as a middleman. Let’s say you’re training for a marathon and you want to make sure you fuel yourself appropriately. Well, if you’re under-eating, you’ll start to lose weight. When you start to see the scale trending downward, that’s your signal to add a few hundred calories to your diet. If, after that adjustment, your weight stays steady, then you know you’re eating the right amount. As you increase your training (or if you take time off to rest a sprained ankle), you can make more adjustments as you go. I have a post here detailing how to make these adjustments with the help of either a paid app, a group of free apps, or a DIY spreadsheet. If you’ve been using a fitness tracker instead, and it’s working for you, feel free to keep using it. But if the tracker ever stops giving you the results you want, you can safely leave it out of the equation.

title: You Could Lose Your Access to 'Old Reddit' Forever, but There's a Workaround
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        October 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Tim Goode/PA Images via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Reddit is making changes to how users can access Old Reddit, the legacy version of the site.
                                            Soon, users will need to use Old Reddit once every six months, otherwise they'll lose access.
                                            Reddit previously made Old Reddit accessible only to logged-in users back in July.
                                            One workaround is to become a mod, since moderators won't have to adhere to this new change.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        "Old Reddit" is the only way I use Reddit. That's not the case for most of the tech in my life. I don't make a point of only using an iPhone from a decade ago, or avoid playing video games with more than 64 bits. But, in my view, Old Reddit is the only proper way to use the website. While "new" Reddit has more "features," it's bloated and slow. Old Reddit might be extremely basic, and looks about the same as it did when I first started "redditing," but it works. Unfortunately, most of us likely won't be able to experience Old Reddit for much longer. On Wednesday, Reddit announced a series of infrastructure changes on its r/modnews subreddit. Normally, these updates wouldn't make tech headlines—I can't say Reddit "mod news" often finds its way into my feeds. But as part of these changes, Reddit confirmed a rather massive deprecation: Users will lose access to Old Reddit unless they've used the platform sometime in the last six months. It's not enough to use Reddit itself, mind you: Unless you use Old Reddit at least once in a six-month period, you'll lose access for good. This builds on a previous Old Reddit change the company rolled out over the summer, which requires users to be logged in in order to access this version of Reddit. While we don't have a true deadline for when these new changes take effect, the new announcement makes it clear that, "in the next few months, we’ll further limit access for logged-in users to only those who have used Old Reddit in the last six months (which covers the vast majority of all Old Reddit users).” The only exception is for moderators.
Why is Reddit going after Old Reddit?According to Reddit, these changes are designed to prevent abuse on its platform. By forcing users to log in to use Old Reddit, the company says it prevents unauthenticated access, its "largest source of abusive scraping and automated traffic." By blocking accounts that haven't accessed Old Reddit in the past six months, Reddit says it's solving another problem: Now, bad actors won't be able to make Reddit accounts for the sole purpose of accessing (and scraping) Old Reddit and its content. In Reddit's view, these changes don't affect Old Reddit users. If you rely on Old Reddit, the company thinks you'll be using it frequently enough to bypass these new rules. As such, Reddit believes the vast majority of affected users will only be those trying to abuse Old Reddit, not those who actively use it. The problem is, not everyone who uses Old Reddit is so steadfast. These new rules mean you can no longer take an extended break from Old Reddit and expect to return in the future. Sure, Reddit will always be there, but you'll lose access to the "best" version of the platform, as so many believe it to be. As this is the second change to Old Reddit in a short period of time, it begs the question: Is Reddit trying to shut down Old Reddit? That's what Ars Technica asked the company, and received the following in response:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
"As [Reddit CEO Steve Huffman previously] confirmed, Reddit is continuing to work on the future of Old Reddit. This change is about limiting unauthenticated access and reducing automated abuse—not removing Old Reddit for people and moderators who rely on it. We want to preserve Old Reddit for the real people that use it, not let it be a vector for automated abuse."How to continue using Old Reddit  Per the rules, the easiest way to continue using Old Reddit is to simply keep using it. If you've never done so before, you can head to old.reddit.com and sign into your account when prompted. As long as you access this version of the site at least once every six months, you'll maintain your access—assuming Reddit doesn't change the rules again.But if you want a more permanent fix without having to worry about visiting Old Reddit twice a year, become a mod. Moderators don't have the same requirements; simply being a mod gives them perpetual access to the site. The easiest way to become a mod is to simply start your own subreddit. If you have access to Old Reddit, you'll see this on the front page as "Create your own subreddit." If you're on new Reddit, you'll see this as "Start a community" under the three-lined menu. Reddit will walk you through the rest, asking you to answer questions or fill out responses about your new community. Assuming the subreddit isn't already taken, you'll be able to create it at the end, at which point you will automatically become a mod of your new subreddit.

title: I Tried Siri AI on My New Apple Watch, and I'm Frustrated
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

            Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        One of the big features Apple announced alongside the new Apple Watches is Siri AI—now available on your wrist! You need to join a waitlist to try Apple's new and improved chatbot, and since my turn just came up, I put the new on-wrist Siri through its paces. Here's how it went, and why I don't think the experience lives up to Apple's promises (yet, anyway).
What devices have Siri AI? Since Siri AI requires Apple Intelligence, you’ll need a device that supports it. Those include iPhones 15 Pro and newer, and an Apple Watch that is Series 9 or newer. If you want to use Siri AI on the Apple Watch, you need both a supported watch and a supported phone—a new watch and old phone won’t do the trick. With my phone and watch both on iOS 27 (the iOS 27.2 developer beta on the phone; watchOS 27.0 on the Apple Watch Series 12), I enabled Siri AI in my phone’s Settings app, which put me on a waiting list. A few days later, I got a notification that I was in. Siri AI on the Apple Watch is occasionally useful, but mostly disappointingOnce I'd upgraded to Siri AI on my watch, I went about asking it plenty of questions and watched it struggle to answer many of them. The first thing I tried was to ask where I could find the nearest yoga studio; it responded with a list of yoga studios, none of them particularly close to my home. After rewording my question a few times, it finally listed one about a mile away. This is one of those examples where using AI is less efficient than a Google search—or even plain old regular Siri: When I asked this same question of the old Siri model last week, it quickly found the closest studio. 
With my phone in another room, I next decided to try some of the questions that Apple provides as examples on the WatchOS 27 page. Here’s how that went. “What’s a good warm-up for deadlifts?” Siri gave me paragraphs of text about the purpose of warmups in general. When I tapped "Show More," I was sent to the bottom of a long bulleted list of exercises. I’m not reading all that.“Read my upcoming events.” Siri needed a good five seconds to think about this one, but then correctly rattled off my next few calendar appointments. “Set a new move ring goal.” Actually, I first started by asking what my Move ring goal was, and Siri could not tell me. So I blindly set a new goal, and later saw it updated to the new value in the Fitness app...sort of. When I asked for a goal of burning 350 calories, it gave me a goal of 350. When I asked for a goal of 325, Siri responded that it has changed my goal to 325, but when I checked the Fitness app, it showed that my goal had been set to 320 calories.Siri AI sometimes performed well on the Apple Watch, but seemed to do better on my iPhoneI then put Siri AI to the test with a few requests that other Apple Watch users have reported give the chatbot some trouble. The first involved setting a timer; perhaps that function is buggy for some users, but it worked quickly for me. “Siri, set a timer for five minutes” did exactly that, with only a few seconds of waiting. Likewise, “Siri, what’s the weather for today?” brought up the weather forecast instantly. One of the purported new features of Siri AI is its ability to search your emails and messages for information that is relavent to a conversation you're having with it. On the Apple Watch, this doesn’t work for me as well as I would like. First, I asked Siri what my daughter had recently asked me to buy for her. (She is constantly texting me to ask for things.) Siri responded that my daughter had sent me a wish list of LEGO sets on Sept. 12. This is true. But it wasn’t until I specified, “wasn’t there a makeup kit?” that Siri was also able to find that request, which was from Sept. 13. Meanwhile, the iPhone version of Siri AI was able to find the wishlist and makeup kit requests and tell me about them in the same initial response, without the additional prompting. In another test of its search capabilities, I asked who I had sent “Ramona’s dad’s phone number” to. The Watch version of Siri AI found that text message, but was only able to tell me the phone number of the person I had sent it to. Siri AI on the phone, on the other hand, was able to figure out that the person requesting the number had introduced themselves by name earlier in that conversation, and it told me exactly who that person was (even though I had not entered the name into my contacts). Where Siri AI struggles on the Apple WatchStill, plenty of requests don’t work even that well, or don’t work at all. The watch’s Siri app routinely crashes, taking me back to the home screen. Sometimes Siri’s voice breaks up, and it interrupts itself to start its message over again. Good save, but weird to listen to. Sometimes Siri “thinks” for a long time. Many requests take five to 10 seconds, during which time I certainly could grab my phone and look up the answer myself. Whenever Siri is stumped, it searches the web and gives me a sea of unhelpful text. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
For example, I tried to see if Siri could explain a mysterious icon on my watch screen. I asked, “Why is this icon gray?” (in a variety of phrasings to clarify I meant one that I was looking at right now). Instead of telling me anything useful, or explaining that it can't see my watch screen, it read me some text from the Internet about what gray icons mean, in general, as a concept. Another time, I asked it to resume playing my podcast. Instead of starting up my usual podcast app, it told me that Episode 550 of My Favorite Murder had just come out. I don’t like murder podcasts, have never listened to My Favorite Murder in my life, and episode 550 was—now that I check—the third-most-recent episode, not the one that just came out. (The iPhone’s version of Siri AI, on the other hand, happily started my podcast app.)At least one thing worked better on the watch: Both versions of Siri AI said they had no information on my sleep data, but the version on the watch was at least able to tell me what time I had gone to bed and what time I had woken up. That's something.The promised Conversations app likewise did not work as expected. When you press the digital crown on the watch, a mini app picker pops up with Siri in the center, surrounded by a few of your most recent apps. If you scroll down, you get the full list (or grid) as before. Tapping that center button is supposed to show you a list of recent conversations, but mine kept showing me “No conversations.” Later, exactly one conversation showed up there: the one where I asked what a gray icon meant. That was the only question in that conversation, even though I had been conversing with Siri all day. Still a work in progressI like the idea of the new Siri AI, and being able to ask follow-up questions is nice, especially now that I can interrupt the chatbot to clarify my questions. (“Give me two specific warm-up exercises I can do before snatches” got it to stop lecturing me about warm-ups in general.) But the long waits for answers, the frequent crashes, and the bot's inability to access data that is right there on the device are frustrating. Here’s hoping it gets better with the next update.

That said, its 4,400mAh battery is modest for a screen this large, and while its IP48 protection covers water immersion, it does not resist dust, so beach and trail use calls for some care.
